lead: A boost converter is a DC-DC circuit that makes a higher DC output from a lower DC input. It stores energy in an inductor from the source while a switch is on, then opens the switch so the inductor drives current through a diode into the output, in series with the source. The output is always above the input: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D). Boost cells appear in battery-to-rail boosters, power-factor-correction front ends, and step-up chopper drives.
prereq: You need: Buck converter for volt-second balance and ripple formulas, and switch ratings from Ratings, snubber circuits and gate drive circuits.

blocks.text: Draw the boost cell. The source V<sub>s</sub> feeds inductor L. The other end of L joins the switch S and the anode of diode D1. S goes from that node to the return rail. D1 goes to output capacitor C and load R. The load sits across C. The switch is a power MOSFET or IGBT with a gate drive; the diode is a fast power diode.

State ON, switch closed. D1 is reverse biased. L sees V<sub>s</sub>, so the inductor voltage v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>. The inductor current i<sub>L</sub> rises linearly. The output capacitor feeds the load alone.

State OFF, switch open. L forces current through D1 into the output. L is now in series with the source, so v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>. This is negative because V<sub>o</sub> > V<sub>s</sub>. The inductor current falls linearly.

Let T be the switching period in seconds and D = T<sub>on</sub>/T the duty ratio, where T<sub>on</sub> is the on-time and T<sub>off</sub> = T − T<sub>on</sub> is the off-time. Volt-second balance over one period gives the gain:
V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D)
D = 1 − V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>o</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is output voltage in V; V<sub>s</sub> is source voltage in V; D is duty ratio, between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: The gain is at least one and, in theory, grows without limit as D approaches one. A real inductor has winding resistance r<sub>L</sub>, and it carries I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D), so its loss grows fast at high D. Including r<sub>L</sub> gives V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = (1 − D)/[(1 − D)² + r<sub>L</sub>/R]. With r<sub>L</sub> = 1 Ω and R = 100 Ω this peaks at 5 at D = 0.9 and falls beyond it, as the figure shows, so practical boosts keep D below about 0.85. The switch carries the full inductor current, not the load current.

During ON, i<sub>L</sub> rises by ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D·T/L. During OFF, it falls by (V<sub>o</sub> − V<sub>s</sub>)(1 − D)T/L. The two changes are equal because the average v<sub>L</sub> over a period is zero.
ΔIL = Vs·D/(fs·L)
ΔI<sub>L</sub> is peak-to-peak inductor ripple current in A; f<sub>s</sub> = 1/T is switching frequency in Hz; L is inductance in H.
I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D)
blocks.where: I<sub>L</sub> is average inductor current in A; I<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>/R is load current in A; R is load resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: The switch current is i<sub>L</sub> during T<sub>on</sub> and zero during T<sub>off</sub>. The diode current is zero during T<sub>on</sub> and i<sub>L</sub> during T<sub>off</sub>. So the input current is smooth, because L is in series with the source. The output current is pulsed, because the diode feeds the output only in the off-time. C supplies the load during the on-time.
The inductor current stays continuous if its minimum is above zero. This is continuous conduction mode (CCM). The boundary inductance is:
Lmin = Vs·D·T/(2IL)
L<sub>min</sub> is the CCM boundary inductance in H; T is switching period in s; I<sub>L</sub> is average inductor current in A.
For L below L<sub>min</sub> the converter enters discontinuous conduction mode (DCM) and the gain formula changes. The output ripple from C alone is:
ΔVo = Io·D/(fs·C)
ΔV<sub>o</sub> is output ripple voltage in V; C is output capacitance in F.
This comes from C feeding the load during D·T. Capacitor equivalent series resistance (ESR) adds a step set by the change in capacitor current, so the measured ripple is larger.

sections.h3: Why the loop is slow and where it is used

blocks.text: The control-to-output response has a right-half-plane (RHP) zero. When D rises, the off-time shrinks at once, so the diode delivers current to the output for a shorter part of the cycle. The output voltage dips before the inductor current can build up. A feedback loop must therefore be slower than in a buck converter. Push the crossover too high and the loop can become unstable.

The boost is also called a step-up chopper. It is the cell behind battery-to-rail boosters, where a low battery voltage must feed a higher DC bus. It is also the boost stage in power-factor-correction (PFC) front ends, where the input current is shaped to follow the line voltage. Both uses are taught in Power factor correction (PFC) rectifiers and in Renewable energy and battery storage interfacing. For reversed polarity and step-down/step-up action, see Buck-boost and Cuk converters.

Ratings: the switch and the diode each block V<sub>o</sub> plus margin and carry I<sub>L</sub> in their part of the cycle. The diode must be fast, because it turns off as the switch turns on. At high gain the off-time is short, so the diode current is a narrow pulse with a high peak and the output capacitor carries a large ripple current.

examples.question: A boost converter runs from a 24 V source with duty ratio D = 0.6, switching frequency f<sub>s</sub> = 50 kHz, L = 300 µH, C = 470 µF, and a 100 Ω load. Find V<sub>o</sub>, I<sub>o</sub>, the average and peak-to-peak ripple inductor current, the minimum and maximum inductor current, and the output ripple.
steps: ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D·T/L = 24 V × 0.6 × 20.0 µs/300 µH = 0.96 A.

i<sub>L,max</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 = 1.5 A + 0.48 A = 1.98 A; i<sub>L,min</sub> = 1.5 A − 0.48 A = 1.02 A. Both are positive, so the converter is in continuous conduction mode (CCM).
ΔV<sub>o</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>·D/(f<sub>s</sub>·C) = 0.6 A × 0.6/(50 kHz × 470 µF) = 0.0153 V = 15.3 mV.
examples.answer: With T = 20.0 µs, V<sub>o</sub> = 60.0 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 0.6 A, I<sub>L</sub> = 1.5 A with ΔI<sub>L</sub> = 0.96 A (1.02 A to 1.98 A), and ΔV<sub>o</sub> = 15.3 mV; the converter is in CCM.

traps: Writing V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D or V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 + D). The boost gain is V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D), so D = 1 − V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>o</sub>.
Forgetting the (1 − D) in the current transfer. The average inductor current is I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D), and the switch carries I<sub>L</sub>, not I<sub>o</sub>.
Saying the diode conducts during the on-time. It is reverse biased then; it conducts only during the off-time.
Using the buck ripple formula. In a boost the inductor sees V<sub>s</sub> during the on-time, so ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D·T/L.
Ignoring the output capacitor duty. C alone feeds the load during the on-time, giving ΔV<sub>o</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>·D/(f<sub>s</sub>·C); ESR makes the measured ripple larger.

quiz.q: Write the boost gain formula and the duty-ratio form.
Why is the output voltage always greater than the input in CCM?
quiz.a: The inductor is charged from V<sub>s</sub>, then connected in series with V<sub>s</sub> through the diode. The output receives the source plus the inductor induced voltage, so the gain 1/(1 − D) is at least one.

quiz.q: A boost has V<sub>s</sub> = 12 V, D = 0.5, f<sub>s</sub> = 100 kHz, L = 100 µH. Find V<sub>o</sub> and ΔI<sub>L</sub>.
A boost delivers 48 V from 12 V into a 0.5 A load. Find D and the average inductor current.
Why is the input current smooth but the output current pulsed?
quiz.a: L is in series with the source, so the source current is i<sub>L</sub>. The diode connects L to the output only during the off-time, so the output current is a pulse.

quiz.q: Why does the right-half-plane zero make the boost loop slower than a buck loop?
quiz.a: A step up in D shortens the off-time and immediately reduces the diode current delivered to the output. V<sub>o</sub> initially falls while i<sub>L</sub> rises. The loop must wait for i<sub>L</sub>, so the crossover must be low.

quiz.q: What happens if D is pushed to 0.95 in a real boost?
quiz.a: The ideal gain is 20, but switch and winding losses and diode drop dominate. Useful gain is less, efficiency falls, and the switch carries a large I<sub>L</sub>. Keep D below about 0.9.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, boost cells sit inside power-factor-correction chips, LED drivers, and battery-to-bus converters. Researchers work on interleaved boosts, bidirectional boost legs for electric vehicles, and wide-band-gap switches that push f<sub>s</sub> higher. The right-half-plane zero is a standard reason to use current-mode control or a slower outer loop. Search for 'boost converter right-half-plane zero', 'interleaved PFC boost', and 'bidirectional DC-DC boost'.
